Well, connected to the real world... I mean, what is the real world, doctor? Because what I see, what I know is happening, it is very real. It's as real as the mop bucket or the brass keys. I know they've marked me. I know it. It started a few weeks ago, or maybe a month, time gets a little slippery. But I noticed the hallway lights on the fourth floor. And then, when I'd see the daytime staff leaving as I was coming in for my shift, they would give each other these little looks. Not big looks, not pointing, but just a tiny shift of the eyes, a little nod, right as they passed me. It was a warning. They were warning each other about me, letting the whole network know I was in the building. 

I tried to show my supervisor. I took him right to the security room, where they have all the monitors lined up, the ones that show every hallway and elevator. I made him pull up the footage from the fourth floor at 6:15 PM, right when the daytime people leave. I said, "Look, look at the lights, look at how they look at each other." And he played the tape back, and he pointed at the screen, and he said, "There's nothing there, Frank. The lights are steady, and those people didn't even look at you." He showed me the camera, plain as day. He said it was all in my head.

The tape doesn't change what I know is happening. The real world... my real world has these warnings in it, even if the camera can't catch them. So, I guess... I guess to them, it's not connected to their real world. But to me, it's the most real thing there is. I have to be so careful now when I clean the fourth floor. I have to make sure I don't look directly at the sensors.

Well, affecting my daily life... yes, yes it is. I mean, how could it not, right? When you're carrying around this kind of knowledge, when you know you've been marked, it... it spills over into everything. 

Like my shifts at work. I've actually missed shifts lately. Mr. Henderson, my supervisor, he told me I couldn't come in on Thursday or Friday last week because I was taking too long on the fourth floor, avoiding the sensors, and I lost out on that pay. I've even lost a couple of side cleaning jobs too, the ones I do on the weekends for the small accounting offices down on Elm Street, because they said I wasn't getting the work done and they couldn't rely on me. But I was just trying to be careful! I was trying to explain to them why I had to clean the baseboards in a specific order so the network wouldn't ping, and they just fired me.

And it's not just the work, doctor. It's my whole life. I don't even go to the mosque anymore. I used to go, you know, regular as clockwork, always took my spot near the shoe racks in the back because the draft from the door keeps it cool. But I stopped going to prayers, and I stopped going to my sister's house for the Sunday family gatherings. My sister and my brother-in-law, they actually sat me down and said they just can't depend on me to show up right, or act right. They said they can't understand a single word I'm saying when I try to explain the warnings and the lights, that I just confuse everyone and upset the nieces and nephews. So I just stopped joining them. It's easier that way, just staying away from people so I don't have to see them looking at me.

But even then, even when I'm alone, sometimes it gets so heavy, this feeling that they're watching and warning each other. It gets so overwhelming that I don't even know what I'm doing, and things get bad. There was a time just recently, out by the loading dock... I got so caught up in the patterns and trying to stop them from tracking me that I guess I got really unsafe. I don't remember all of it perfectly, just the freezing cold air and my heart hammering in my chest, but I was out by the dumpsters in just my undershirt in the middle of the night. I was trying to dismantle the security floodlights with a broken mop handle, and the night guard had to call for emergency help. They actually had to call an ambulance and the police to come get me because they said I was a danger to myself, slipping on the ice and screaming at the brick wall. So yes, it... it affects everything. Everything is broken now because of it.

Well, sticking to one topic... yes, that is... honestly, doctor, that is exactly what brings me here. My talking, it just gets all mixed up lately. I don't mean for it to happen, I really don't, but there is just so much going on up here and it all needs to come out at once so people can understand the whole picture.

The green prayer rug with the gold fringe that I used to kneel on before the network started tracking me. And from the prayer rug, well, it just naturally leads me to the chess pieces. The knights and the pawns, the way they move in specific patterns across the board, jumping over things just like how I have to move down the hallways to avoid the sensors. 

To me, doctor, it is a perfectly straight line. One thing leads right into the exact next thing, clear as day. But when the words actually come out of my mouth, people just look at me like I am speaking a completely different language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. My sister does it, Mr. Henderson does it... they just rub their temples or shake their heads and tell me I am jumping all over the place, going from the keys to the jail to the rug to the chess pieces. They say I am not making any sense and they just cannot keep up with my sentences. 

But I have to explain all of it! If I leave out the chess pieces, then the prayer rug doesn't make sense, and if I don't talk about the jail, you won't understand the keys. There are just so many pieces to the puzzle, and I try so hard to give them the whole picture so they can see what I see, but they just get frustrated. They tell me I am confusing them and they stop listening to me, and I am just left standing there in the hallway trying to finish the thought, trying to show them how it all connects... but the words just keep getting tangled up.

But they weren't just clicking on when I walked by. They were flickering in a pattern. Three fast, one slow. And then, when I'd see the daytime staff leaving as I was coming in for my shift, they would give each other these little looks. Not big looks, not pointing, but just a tiny shift of the eyes, a little nod, right as they passed me. It was a warning. They were warning each other about me, letting the whole network know I was in the building. \n\nI tried to show my supervisor. I took him right to the security room, where they have all the monitors lined up, the ones that show every hallway and elevator. I made him pull up the footage from the fourth floor at 6:15 PM, right when the daytime people leave. I said, \"Look, look at the lights, look at how they look at each other.\" And he played the tape back, and he pointed at the screen, and he said, \"There's nothing there, Frank. The lights are steady, and those people didn't even look at you.\" He showed me the camera, plain as day. He said it was all in my head. \n\nBut... but even when he showed me that, even when I saw the tape with my own two eyes and it looked perfectly normal... I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. The tape doesn't change what I know is happening. The real world... my real world has these warnings in it, even if the camera can't catch them. So, I guess... I guess to them, it's not connected to their real world. But to me, it's the most real thing there is. I have to be so careful now when I clean the fourth floor. I have to make sure I don't look directly at the sensors.\n\nDoctor: Do you really believe that the people in the building have marked you, or is that just a feeling you have?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it’s... it’s not just a passing feeling, like when you feel a chill because someone left the loading dock door open. No, it’s... I know it. I absolutely believe it, down to my very bones. I know it sounds crazy to you, and I know my supervisor—Mr. Henderson, he's been there fifteen years, always wears those short-sleeved button-downs no matter how cold it gets—I know he showed me that security tape. \n\nWe were standing right there in the little room with all the monitors, and the room always smells like stale coffee and ozone from all the electronics, and he pointed right at the screen. He rewound it, played it, rewound it again. And I looked at it, I really did. I stared at that little glowing square, and I saw what he saw. The lights weren't flickering three fast, one slow. The people in the suits, they were just walking to the elevators, looking at their phones or whatever it is they do. \n\nBut even seeing that... even staring right at the proof that nothing was happening... it didn't change a thing in here, in my head, in my gut. I still felt it. I still feel it right now. I am completely, one hundred percent sure they have marked me. The tape is just... it's just a tape, you know? It only catches the surface of things. It doesn't catch the truth of what's happening. The little looks, the warnings, the way the network operates... it's real. It's so real that I have to change my whole routine. I have to push my cart down the left side of the hall, keeping my head down, making sure I don't trigger whatever system they have set up. So yes, I believe it. I believe it more than I believe that the sun is going to come up tomorrow, no matter what that camera showed.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the beliefs you have about being marked are affecting your daily life in any significant way?\n\nPatient: Well, affecting my daily life... yes, yes it is. But I was just trying to be careful! I was trying to explain to them why I had to clean the baseboards in a specific order so the network wouldn't ping, and they just fired me.\n\nAnd it's not just the work, doctor. It's my whole life. My sister and my brother-in-law, they actually sat me down and said they just can't depend on me to show up right, or act right. The knights and the pawns, the way they move in specific patterns across the board, jumping over things just like how I have to move down the hallways to avoid the sensors. \n\nTo me, doctor, it is a perfectly straight line. One thing leads right into the exact next thing, clear as day. But when the words actually come out of my mouth, people just look at me like I am speaking a completely different language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. My sister does it, Mr. Henderson does it... they just rub their temples or shake their heads and tell me I am jumping all over the place, going from the keys to the jail to the rug to the chess pieces. They say I am not making any sense and they just cannot keep up with my sentences. \n\nBut I have to explain all of it! ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no, doctor... no, it hasn't always been this way. I used to be a very quiet man, you know? I just kept my head down, pushed my broom, emptied the bins, and went home. But this... this rush in my head, the way the words all pile up and spill out tangled together... that started about two years and five months ago. Exactly two years and five months, actually. It was right after... well, right after that brief detention I had, over the misunderstanding at the building. 

You see, it was just a misunderstanding, but it changed everything. I was down near the south stairwell, just trying to arrange the wet floor signs in a specific triangle so the sensors wouldn't trip and track me, and the night security—the guys with the heavy boots and the radios on their shoulders that always hiss static—they didn't understand what I was doing. They thought I was doing something wrong, tampering with the fire doors or something. So they detained me. They called it just a brief detention, but they put me in this little concrete room down by the boiler. It was so hot in there, doctor, and it smelled like burnt dust and industrial bleach, and they just left me sitting there on this cold metal folding chair while they tried to figure it out. 

And while I was sitting there, just listening to the pipes groan and feeling the vibrations from the boiler right through the rubber soles of my work boots... that’s when my mind just... it just started racing. I realized how close I came to being locked away for good, like in a real jail, all because they didn't understand the patterns and the warnings. I realized I hadn't been explaining it right. When they finally let me go, when Mr. Henderson finally came down and cleared it all up as a misunderstanding and said I was just the janitor... my head wasn't the same. 

Ever since then, for two years and five months now, my brain has been running like a floor buffer that won't shut off. I never used to talk this much, but now I have to, because if I don't, they might misunderstand again. They might lock me in that basement room again and leave me there. So I talk, and I think, and I try to lay out all the pieces for people—the keys, the rug, the sensors—but it all gets jumbled up because there's just so much to say and so much they need to know to keep me safe. So, no, it wasn't always like this. Just since that night they detained me. That's when the tangling started, two years and five months ago, and it just hasn't stopped since.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, connected in a logical way... I don't know about logical, doctor, because to me, maybe there is a logic in there somewhere, but it's really about the speed. It's the sheer speed of it all that makes it so hard. My thoughts, they just run so fast. It's not just one quiet thought at a time like it used to be. One second I'm thinking about my bills, you know, the stack of envelopes sitting on my kitchen table, worrying about the electric bill and how I lost those weekend cleaning jobs. And then, before I can even finish figuring out the math for the electricity, my brain is suddenly jumping straight to the jail. I'm right back in that concrete room thinking about being locked up, feeling the cold metal chair. And then, bam, it's not the jail anymore, it jumps right to the mosque. I'm suddenly thinking about the gold fringe on the prayer rug and the cool draft by the shoe racks in the back, wondering why I stopped going. And then, just as fast as that, my mind is completely wrapped up in cleaning chemicals. The smell of the industrial bleach, the heavy ammonia I use on the tiles, worrying if the mix is right or if it's going to leave a film on the floor that the sensors will pick up. 

It just jumps and jumps and jumps—from the bills, to the jail, to the mosque, to the cleaning chemicals—just bouncing around inside my skull. It goes so incredibly fast that before I can even catch one single thought, before I can grab hold of the worry about the bills and actually do something about it, the crowd in my head has already moved on to the bleach and the prayers. I try to reach out and stop them, to just hold onto one idea for a minute, but I can't catch a single one of them. It is so exhausting, doctor, it really is, just trying to keep up with my own brain when it is sprinting away from me like that from the moment I wake up until I finally pass out.

It started a few weeks ago, or maybe a month, time gets a little slippery. But I noticed the hallway lights on the fourth floor. They have these motion sensors, right? But they weren't just clicking on when I walked by. They were flickering in a pattern. Three fast, one slow. And then, when I'd see the daytime staff leaving as I was coming in for my shift, they would give each other these little looks. Not big looks, not pointing, but just a tiny shift of the eyes, a little nod, right as they passed me. It was a warning. They were warning each other about me, letting the whole network know I was in the building. \n\nI tried to show my supervisor. I took him right to the security room, where they have all the monitors lined up, the ones that show every hallway and elevator. I made him pull up the footage from the fourth floor at 6:15 PM, right when the daytime people leave. I said, \"Look, look at the lights, look at how they look at each other.\" And he played the tape back, and he pointed at the screen, and he said, \"There's nothing there, Frank. The lights are steady, and those people didn't even look at you.\" He showed me the camera, plain as day. He said it was all in my head. \n\nBut... but even when he showed me that, even when I saw the tape with my own two eyes and it looked perfectly normal... I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. The tape doesn't change what I know is happening. The real world... my real world has these warnings in it, even if the camera can't catch them. So, I guess... I guess to them, it's not connected to their real world. But to me, it's the most real thing there is. I have to be so careful now when I clean the fourth floor. I have to make sure I don't look directly at the sensors.\n\nDoctor: Do you really believe that the people in the building have marked you, or is that just a feeling you have?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it’s... it’s not just a passing feeling, like when you feel a chill because someone left the loading dock door open. No, it’s... I know it. I absolutely believe it, down to my very bones. I know it sounds crazy to you, and I know my supervisor—Mr. Henderson, he's been there fifteen years, always wears those short-sleeved button-downs no matter how cold it gets—I know he showed me that security tape. \n\nWe were standing right there in the little room with all the monitors, and the room always smells like stale coffee and ozone from all the electronics, and he pointed right at the screen. He rewound it, played it, rewound it again. And I looked at it, I really did. I stared at that little glowing square, and I saw what he saw. The lights weren't flickering three fast, one slow. The people in the suits, they were just walking to the elevators, looking at their phones or whatever it is they do. \n\nBut even seeing that... even staring right at the proof that nothing was happening... it didn't change a thing in here, in my head, in my gut. I still felt it. I still feel it right now. I am completely, one hundred percent sure they have marked me. The tape is just... it's just a tape, you know? It only catches the surface of things. It doesn't catch the truth of what's happening. The little looks, the warnings, the way the network operates... it's real. It's so real that I have to change my whole routine. I have to push my cart down the left side of the hall, keeping my head down, making sure I don't trigger whatever system they have set up. So yes, I believe it. I believe it more than I believe that the sun is going to come up tomorrow, no matter what that camera showed.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the beliefs you have about being marked are affecting your daily life in any significant way?\n\nPatient: Well, affecting my daily life... yes, yes it is. I mean, how could it not, right? When you're carrying around this kind of knowledge, when you know you've been marked, it... it spills over into everything. \n\nLike my shifts at work. I've actually missed shifts lately. I've even lost a couple of side cleaning jobs too, the ones I do on the weekends for the small accounting offices down on Elm Street, because they said I wasn't getting the work done and they couldn't rely on me. Clear and organized? Well, I try, doctor, I really do try to get it all lined up straight in my head before I open my mouth, but... honestly, no. Not lately. Not for a long time. In fact, that's... well, that's exactly what brings me here to see you in the first place.

I'll start off trying to explain about the keys—you know, my heavy brass work keys, the master ring I clip to my belt that opens the utility closets and the freight elevator—and I'm just trying to talk about the keys, but then suddenly the words coming out of my mouth are all about the jail. I'm talking about the gold fringe and the mosque, and then, out of nowhere, I'm trying to explain about chess pieces. Just... chess pieces, the knights and the pawns, moving them around, and I don't even play chess, but the words just keep tumbling out of me, one right after the other, all tangled up in this big, heavy knot. 

And I look at the person I'm talking to—like my supervisor Mr. Henderson, or the people at the front desk, or the nurses here—and they just have this blank, confused look on their faces. They just stare at me, maybe tilt their heads. And they tell me... they tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They hold up their hands and say, "Slow down, you're not making any sense, we can't follow you." 

But to me, I'm just trying to get it all out! I'm trying to explain the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces, because it's all rushing at me at once and I need them to hear it. It's like I'm speaking a completely different language, doctor, and I just can't make it stop and be clear, no matter how hard I try to just say one simple, normal sentence. It just keeps spilling out all mixed up, and nobody understands a word of it, and that's why I'm sitting in this chair right now.

They tell me I am confusing them and they stop listening to me, and I am just left standing there in the hallway trying to finish the thought, trying to show them how it all connects... but the words just keep getting tangled up.\n\nDoctor: Has your way of talking and thinking always been like this, or is this something that has changed over time?\n\nPatient: Well, no, doctor... no, it hasn't always been this way. They called it just a brief detention, but they put me in this little concrete room down by the boiler. I realized how close I came to being locked away for good, like in a real jail, all because they didn't understand the patterns and the warnings. I realized I hadn't been explaining it right. When they finally let me go, when Mr. Henderson finally came down and cleared it all up as a misunderstanding and said I was just the janitor... my head wasn't the same. \n\nEver since then, for two years and five months now, my brain has been running like a floor buffer that won't shut off. I never used to talk this much, but now I have to, because if I don't, they might misunderstand again. They might lock me in that basement room again and leave me there. So I talk, and I think, and I try to lay out all the pieces for people—the keys, the rug, the sensors—but it all gets jumbled up because there's just so much to say and so much they need to know to keep me safe. So, no, it wasn't always like this. Just since that night they detained me. That's when the tangling started, two years and five months ago, and it just hasn't stopped since.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself having thoughts that are not connected to each other in a logical way?\n\nPatient: Well, connected in a logical way... My thoughts, they just run so fast. It's not just one quiet thought at a time like it used to be. I'm right back in that concrete room thinking about being locked up, feeling the cold metal chair. And then, bam, it's not the jail anymore, it jumps right to the mosque. I'm suddenly thinking about the gold fringe on the prayer rug and the cool draft by the shoe racks in the back, wondering why I stopped going. Finding the right words? No, no, doctor, it's not that I can't find the words. The words are all there, there are just... there are too many of them, and they're moving so fast. They thought I was doing something wrong, tampering with the fire doors or something. So they detained me. When they finally let me go, when Mr. Henderson finally came down and cleared it all up as a misunderstanding and said I was just the janitor... my head wasn't the same. \n\nEver since then, for two years and five months now, my brain has been running like a floor buffer that won't shut off. I never used to talk this much, but now I have to, because if I don't, they might misunderstand again. They might lock me in that basement room again and leave me there. So I talk, and I think, and I try to lay out all the pieces for people—the keys, the rug, the sensors—but it all gets jumbled up because there's just so much to say and so much they need to know to keep me safe. So, no, it wasn't always like this. Just since that night they detained me. That's when the tangling started, two years and five months ago, and it just hasn't stopped since.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself having thoughts that are not connected to each other in a logical way?\n\nPatient: Well, connected in a logical way... I try to reach out and stop them, to just hold onto one idea for a minute, but I can't catch a single one of them. And when I ask Mr. Henderson on patrol, when I ask if he heard the man shouting in the closet, he just shakes his head and tells me the building is empty. But I know what I heard. It's a real voice, doctor, standing right there in the room with me, even when nobody is there.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the voice you hear is trying to tell you something important about your situation, or is it just a noise in your head?\n\nPatient: Important? It’s trying to tell me what I already know deep down, what I see with my own eyes every single shift. \n\nI actually went to my supervisor about it. I went to Mr. Henderson, and I tried to explain what was going on, and he took me back into the main security office—the one with the big bank of monitors that always smell like hot ozone and stale coffee. They are warning each other that I'm there, that I'm the one who ruined everything, exactly like the voice in the vent keeps saying. \n\nSo Mr. Henderson can point at his blank camera screens all he wants, but the cameras don't catch the rhythm of the lights, and they don't catch those little looks they pass around. The voice isn't just noise in my head, doctor. It's the truth. It just keeps spilling out all mixed up, and nobody understands a word of it, and that's why I'm sitting in this chair right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find it difficult to express your thoughts in a coherent and orderly manner?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, doctor, that's... that's exactly what I was just trying to tell you a moment ago. I'll haul out the heavy machinery, the big floor buffers, the buckets, the gallons of stripper, and I'll just start tearing into it. I feel like I absolutely cannot slow down. My motor is just running way too hot, way too fast, and it stays like that for weeks and weeks. So no, extended clear time? That's just... that's just not my reality anymore. It's mostly just this... this endless, driven pushing.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have control over your thoughts, or do they seem to have a life of their own?\n\nPatient: Control? Doctor, control is a word that belongs to someone else's life, not mine. Not anymore. I try to hold on, I really do, but my thoughts... they absolutely have a life of their own. They don't just have a life of their own, they have a whole city of their own in there! \n\nIt's like... it's like my brain is an engine that's had the governor taken off, and someone just put a brick on the gas pedal. The thoughts run so fast, just incredibly fast. It feels exactly like there is an entire crowd of people standing inside my head, all shouting at the same time. And they're not even talking about the same thing! One second, I'm trying to figure out how I'm going to pay the electric bill, because they sent the red notice, you know, the one with the big bold letters at the top, and before I can even finish worrying about the bill, my mind has already jumped to the jail. I'm thinking about the bars and the cold concrete from back then, and then—bam!—it’s gone, and suddenly I'm thinking about the mosque, about the prayer rugs and the way the light comes through the windows during Friday prayers, and then before I can even picture the rug properly, I'm obsessing over the exact mixing ratio of the industrial floor stripper and the ammonia cleaner! \n\nIt's exhausting, doctor, it really is. It’s bills, jail, mosque, chemicals, over and over, faster and faster, and I'm just standing there holding my mop, trying to catch just one single thought, just trying to grab onto one of them so I can finish a sentence or finish a job. But I can't catch them. They just blur past me. So no, I don't have control. They are driving the bus, and I'm just getting dragged along behind it, bouncing off the pavement.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the voice you hear is a part of your own mind or something separate from you?\n\nPatient: Separate. Definitely separate. It's not my mind playing tricks on me, doctor, it's not like when you get a song stuck in your head and you can't get it out. No, no, this is... it's completely outside of me. \n\nI hear him so clearly. It's a man's voice, always a man, and he's either up in the vents like I told you, or sometimes... sometimes he's right inside the mop closet with me. I'll be in there, you know, the one on the third floor next to the freight elevator, it's a tight space, barely enough room for the cart and the sink. I'll be in there mixing the chemicals, trying to focus, trying to ignore the racing thoughts, and suddenly I'll hear him. He'll just say my name. Just my name, real low, but so clear. Or worse, he'll start telling me that I ruined everything. \"You ruined it all,\" he'll say. And doctor, I swear to you, it sounds exactly as real as you sitting there talking to me right now. It's not a thought, it's a sound. It's a real sound hitting my ears. \n\nIf it was just my own mind, wouldn't I be able to turn it off? Wouldn't I be able to say, \"Hey, stop saying that, I didn't ruin everything\"? But I can't. Because he's not me. He's somewhere in the building, in the walls, in the closet... I don't know how he gets in there, but he's there, and he's talking to me, and it's terrifying because I can't ever find him when I look. I'll swing the closet door wide open, I'll shine my flashlight up into the grate, but there's no one. Just the voice. Just that awful voice telling me I ruined everything, sounding as real as the floor buffer humming. So yes, separate. Absolutely separate from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find it difficult to stick to one topic when you're talking to someone?\n\nPatient: Stick to one topic? Yeah... yeah, that's... actually, that's exactly what brings me here, to be honest. My talking, it just gets all mixed up. I'll be trying to have a normal conversation, maybe with the night supervisor or one of the guards, and I'll start off talking about the supply closet keys, you know, the heavy brass ones on the big metal ring. I try to explain about the keys, but then my mouth just keeps going and suddenly I'm talking about the jail, about how the keys there sounded when the guards walked by the cells and that heavy clinking sound. \n\nAnd then from the jail, I'm suddenly talking about the prayer rug, the one at the mosque, because I was thinking about kneeling on the cold concrete versus kneeling on the soft rug, and then before I can even finish explaining that part, I'm trying to tell them about chess pieces! Because the way the keys clink together, it sounds exactly like when you knock a rook against a knight on a heavy wooden board. \n\nIt all makes perfect sense in my head, doctor, it really does, the connections are all right there. But when I'm standing there talking, the supervisor or whoever I've got cornered by the elevators, they just look at me like I have two heads. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They literally put their hands up, like this, and say, \"Whoa, slow down, I can't follow you, what are you even talking about?\" And I get so frustrated because I'm trying to explain the whole picture to them, how the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces all tie together, but they just get this confused look and walk away. They say my talking is just too mixed up to understand. It’s like I can’t just say one simple thing anymore, I have to say everything all at once, and it just spills out in this big tangled mess.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of time where your thoughts were clear and organized, but then you suddenly experienced a dramatic change in your thinking and behavior?\n\nPatient: Clear? Oh, yeah... yeah, I used to have a very clear head. I used to just go in, clock my hours, push my cart, and my mind was my own. It was quiet. Organized, just like my supply closet used to be, everything in its proper place, all the bottles lined up with the labels facing out. But that... that feels like a whole lifetime ago now. \n\nBecause this whole nightmare, this sudden shift where everything just went completely off the rails... it's been going on for about two years and five months now. Two years and five months of this constant noise. And I know exactly when it started, doctor, I know the exact turning point. It was right after this... this whole ridiculous misunderstanding at the building. \n\nI was just doing my job, you know, working the night shift, taking care of the lower concourse near the freight elevators, and there was this huge confusion with the new security team. They thought I was somewhere I wasn't supposed to be, or doing something with the electrical panels—it was a complete misunderstanding, I swear to you. I was just trying to mop up a spill near the utility boxes! But they overreacted. They got management involved, they called the police, and I went through this brief detention. They actually took me in! Just for a little while, just a brief detention down at the station until they got the story straight and realized I was just the building cleaner doing my regular route and let me go. \n\nBut sitting in that room, that cold concrete holding cell... something just... snapped. Or shifted. When I walked out of there, when I went back to the building after that, nothing was the same. Before that misunderstanding, I could think straight. I could plan out my whole shift. But that was two years and five months ago, and ever since that exact day, my thoughts haven't been clear at all. They just started racing and tumbling, the voices, the mixed-up words, all of it just exploded right after they let me out. So yeah, it was a dramatic change, a very dramatic change, and it hasn't stopped for a single second since that detention."
